title: Statutory Security Deposit Protections & Timelines
citation: Uniform Residential Landlord & Tenant Act (URLTA) § 2.101 / Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5
text: Landlords are statutorily required to return tenant security deposits within strict statutory deadlines (typically 14 to 30 days depending on jurisdiction) accompanied by an itemized written statement detailing any lawful deductions. Deductions are strictly limited to unpaid rent, cleaning necessary to restore premises to move-in condition, and repair of damages exceeding ordinary wear and tear. Bad-faith retention by the landlord entitles the tenant to statutory treble damages plus attorney fees.
key_elements: Return deadline: 14–30 days
Mandatory itemized deduction statement
Ordinary wear and tear cannot be deducted
Bad faith entitles tenant to statutory penalties/damages
action_checklist: Send formal written demand letter via certified mail
Provide photos/videos of move-out condition
File small claims court action if unresolved within 30 days

title: Implied Warranty of Habitability & Constructive Eviction
citation: Restatement (Second) of Property § 5.5 / Javins v. First National Realty Corp.
text: Every residential lease incorporates an non-waivable implied warranty of habitability requiring the landlord to maintain hot and cold running water, functioning heating, weather-tight roofing and windows, safe electrical wiring, clean sanitary facilities, and freedom from toxic mold or vermin infestations. If a landlord fails to remedy substantial code violations within reasonable notice (typically 14 days), the tenant may withhold rent into an escrow account, repair and deduct, or vacate under the doctrine of constructive eviction.
key_elements: Non-waivable implied warranty in residential leases
Mandatory working heat, water, weatherproofing, plumbing
Right to repair-and-deduct or escrow rent upon written notice
Constructive eviction if premises become uninhabitable
action_checklist: Document code violations with time-stamped photographs
Deliver written notice to landlord demanding remedy within 14 days
Contact municipal housing or code enforcement inspectors for formal inspection report

title: Fifth & Sixth Amendment Protections & Miranda Admissibility
citation: U.S. Const. amends. V, VI / Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966)
text: Prior to any custodial interrogation, law enforcement officers must advise an individual of their constitutional rights: the right to remain silent, that any statement made can and will be used against them in court, the right to the presence of an attorney, and that an attorney will be appointed if indigent. Any custodial statements obtained in violation of Miranda are inadmissible in the prosecution's case-in-chief. Invocation of the right to counsel must be unambiguous and immediately halts all questioning.
key_elements: Custodial interrogation triggers mandatory Miranda warning
Statements made during unlawful questioning are subject to suppression
Clear unambiguous invocation immediately halts interrogation
Right to court-appointed counsel during critical proceedings
action_checklist: Politely state: 'I am exercising my right to remain silent and I want an attorney'
Sign no waivers, written confessions, or consent-to-search documents without counsel
Retain experienced criminal defense counsel before scheduled arraignment

title: Fourth Amendment Warrant Requirement & Exclusionary Rule
citation: U.S. Const. amend. IV / Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961)
text: The Fourth Amendment guarantees individuals the right to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Searches conducted without a judicial warrant issued upon probable cause supported by oath or affirmation are per se unreasonable, subject only to established exceptions (e.g., exigent circumstances, consent, automobile search upon probable cause). Evidence seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment must be excluded from trial under the exclusionary rule.
key_elements: Warrantless searches are presumptively unconstitutional
Probable cause required for lawful search warrants
Exclusionary rule suppresses illegally obtained evidence
Fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine taints secondary evidence
action_checklist: State clearly: 'Officer, I do not consent to any search of my person, car, or home'
Do not physically obstruct law enforcement officers
Request attorney file a formal Motion to Suppress evidence under the 4th Amendment

title: Delaware General Corporation Law & Fiduciary Duties
citation: Del. Code Ann. tit. 8, § 141 / In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation
text: Corporate directors and officers owe strict fiduciary duties of care, loyalty, and good faith to the corporation and its stockholders. The duty of care requires directors to act on an informed basis in the honest belief that actions taken are in the best interests of the company, protected under the Business Judgment Rule. The duty of loyalty prohibits self-dealing, usurping corporate opportunities, and bad-faith conflicts of interest. Breaches of the duty of loyalty cannot be exculpated under corporate charter provisions.
key_elements: Duty of Care and Duty of Loyalty owed by all directors
Business Judgment Rule protects informed, unconflicted board decisions
Prohibition on self-dealing and corporate opportunity usurpation
Shareholder derivative actions for breaches of fiduciary duty
action_checklist: Establish an independent board committee for conflict transactions
Document contemporaneous board minutes and valuation analyses
Maintain robust Directors & Officers (D&O) liability insurance coverage

title: Material Breach, Expectation Damages & Opportunity to Cure
citation: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 241 / Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 2-601
text: A breach of contract is considered material if it deprives the injured party of the fundamental benefit reasonably expected under the agreement. A material breach excuses the non-breaching party from continuing performance and triggers an immediate entitlement to expectation damages designed to place the injured party in the financial position they would have occupied had full performance occurred. Many commercial contracts mandate a written Notice of Default giving the breaching party a 15 to 30 day cure period before filing suit.
key_elements: Material breach excuses injured party from further performance
Entitlement to expectation damages and lost profits
Mandatory written notice and opportunity to cure if stipulated
Duty of non-breaching party to mitigate damages
action_checklist: Review contract terms for express notice and cure period requirements
Issue formal Notice of Default citing specific breach provisions
Quantify documented economic losses and maintain mitigation records

title: Title VII Employment Discrimination & Retaliation Prohibitions
citation: Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e / Burlington Northern v. White
text: Title VII makes it unlawful for employers with 15 or more employees to discriminate in hiring, firing, compensation, terms, or conditions of employment based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. It is strictly unlawful to retaliate against an employee for opposing discriminatory practices, filing a charge, or participating in an investigation. Plaintiffs must exhaust administrative remedies by filing a Charge of Discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) within 180 or 300 days before filing in federal court.
key_elements: Protection against discrimination based on protected classes
Strict prohibition on retaliation against whistleblowers and complainants
Mandatory EEOC filing deadline: 180 to 300 days from adverse action
Remedies include back pay, front pay, compensatory damages, and attorney fees
action_checklist: Preserve all emails, performance reviews, and termination letters
File formal internal complaint with HR in writing to establish protected activity
File timely Charge of Discrimination with EEOC to obtain Right-to-Sue letter

title: Deprivation of Civil Rights Under Color of State Law
citation: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 / Monell v. Department of Social Services
text: Every person who, under color of any state statute, ordinance, regulation, or custom, subjects any citizen or person within the jurisdiction of the United States to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution and laws, shall be liable to the party injured in an action at law or suit in equity. Section 1983 provides the primary federal enforcement vehicle for constitutional torts including excessive force, unlawful arrest, and Fourteenth Amendment due process violations.
key_elements: Color of state law requirement for government officials
Redress for violations of constitutional rights (1st, 4th, 8th, 14th Amendments)
Monell liability for unconstitutional municipal policies or customs
Prevailing plaintiffs entitled to attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988
action_checklist: Preserve all video recordings, body camera footage, and surveillance logs
Obtain medical evaluations documenting physical or psychological trauma
File required municipal administrative claim notices within statutory time limits

title: Tort Negligence Elements & Comparative Fault Doctrines
citation: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 6
text: To establish actionable negligence in personal injury litigation, the plaintiff must prove four fundamental legal elements by a preponderance of the evidence: (1) a legal duty of care owed by defendant to plaintiff, (2) breach of that duty by failure to exercise reasonable care, (3) actual and proximate causation linking defendant's breach to plaintiff's harm, and (4) legally compensable damages. Under comparative negligence rules, plaintiff's recovery is reduced proportionally by their own percentage of fault.
key_elements: Four legal elements: Duty, Breach, Causation, and Damages
Comparative fault reduces damages proportionally
Recovery includes medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering
Statute of limitations typically 2 to 3 years from date of injury
action_checklist: Seek immediate medical treatment and maintain consistent doctor visits
Do not provide recorded audio statements to opposing insurance adjusters
Photograph vehicular impact points, road conditions, and physical injuries

title: Best Interests of the Child Standard & Equitable Distribution
citation: Uniform Marriage and Divorce Act (UMDA) § 402 / Troxel v. Granville
text: Child custody and visitation determinations are governed exclusively by the 'best interests of the child' statutory standard, evaluating parental fitness, emotional bonds, stability of home environment, history of domestic conflict, and each parent's willingness to foster an ongoing relationship between the child and the other parent. Marital assets acquired during the marriage are subject to equitable distribution (or 50/50 division in community property jurisdictions), regardless of whose name appears on the legal title.
key_elements: Paramount legal standard: 'Best interests of the child'
Equitable distribution of all marital property and retirement assets
Child support determined by statutory guideline income models
Presumption favoring frequent and continuous contact with both parents
action_checklist: Compile 3 years of tax returns, bank statements, and pension records
Maintain a neutral parenting time log documenting daily custody schedules
Consult family law counsel before executing any settlement or custody agreement

title: Federal Trademark Infringement & Likelihood of Confusion
citation: Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1114 / Polaroid Corp. v. Polarad Electronics Corp.
text: Under the Lanham Act, trademark infringement occurs when a party uses in commerce any reproduction, counterfeit, copy, or colorable imitation of a registered mark in connection with the sale or advertising of goods or services, where such use is likely to cause consumer confusion, mistake, or deception. Courts evaluate the likelihood of confusion using factors including the strength of plaintiff's mark, similarity of the marks, proximity of the goods in the market, evidence of actual confusion, and defendant's intent.
key_elements: Likelihood of consumer confusion is the core legal standard
Federal registration on USPTO Principal Register grants nationwide priority
Remedies include preliminary injunctions, defendant profits, and treble damages
Defense of non-commercial fair use or descriptive fair use
action_checklist: Conduct USPTO trademark clearance search across identical classes
Document customer inquiries demonstrating actual confusion
Issue formal Cease and Desist demand with proof of priority registration

title: Statutory Notice of Deficiency & U.S. Tax Court Jurisdiction
text: When the Internal Revenue Service determines a tax deficiency, it must mail a formal Notice of Deficiency (90-day letter) via certified mail to the taxpayer's last known address. The taxpayer has exactly 90 days from the mailing date (150 days if addressed outside the U.S.) to file a petition in the United States Tax Court. Filing a timely Tax Court petition prevents the IRS from assessing or collecting the contested tax liability until the court enters a final decision.
key_elements: Strict 90-day statutory jurisdictional deadline to file Tax Court petition
Automatic stay prevents IRS assessment and levy during Tax Court review
Tax Court allows prepayment litigation without paying tax first
Failure to file within 90 days forfeits Tax Court jurisdiction
action_checklist: Calculate the exact 90th day deadline indicated on IRS Letter 531
File Form 2 (Petition) with U.S. Tax Court prior to deadline expiration
Retain a tax attorney or licensed enrolled agent with Power of Attorney (Form 2848)
